## Build with Parmana

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/build-book/overview

This book takes you from nothing to a production integration: an AI agent that can act on a real system only when a
policy and a person allow it, with a signed record of every decision. It is the companion to
[The Parmana Handbook](/handbook/overview), which explains how each part of Parmana is built. This book explains how to
**build with** it.

Download it as one PDF: [build-with-parmana.pdf](/build-with-parmana.pdf).

## Who it is for

| You are                                     | Start with                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A developer connecting an agent             | [Chapter 1](/build-book/01-how-parmana-works), then [Chapter 3](/build-book/03-connect-an-agent)                                          |
| An operator bringing Parmana to production  | [Chapter 8](/build-book/08-deploy-and-operate), then [Chapter 4](/build-book/04-policies) and [Chapter 5](/build-book/05-human-approvals) |
| Connecting a system Parmana has no code for | [Chapter 6](/build-book/06-connect-your-systems)                                                                                          |
| Reviewing Parmana for security              | [Chapter 10](/build-book/10-security-model-and-limits), then [Chapter 7](/build-book/07-verify-and-audit)                                 |
| An AI agent                                 | [Integrate Parmana: specification for AI agents](/agents/integrate), and `llms-full.txt` for this site in one file                        |

## How the book is written

- **Every statement is checked against the code.** Where the book and the code disagree, the code wins and the book
  is fixed. Anything not verified in production says so.
- **The reference chapters are generated from the code.** [Every endpoint](/build-book/reference-endpoints),
  [every SDK method](/build-book/reference-sdk) and [every error code](/build-book/reference-errors) are produced by
  `scripts/generate-build-book-reference.ts` from the OpenAPI file, the SDK source and the server's error classes. A
  test fails when they fall behind the code.
- **Examples are real.** Responses are captured from the running server; tutorial output is what the tutorial prints.
- **Procedures state what to expect.** Where a step can fail, it says what you see and what to do.

## The chapters

1. [How Parmana works](/build-book/01-how-parmana-works): one request, from an agent to a signed record.
2. [Your first governed action](/build-book/02-your-first-governed-action): run it on your machine, step by step.
3. [Connect an agent](/build-book/03-connect-an-agent): the request, the policy in effect, approvals, in both SDKs.
4. [Policies](/build-book/04-policies): write one, get it approved, change it, roll it back.
5. [Human approvals](/build-book/05-human-approvals): approvers, signing, and what an approval covers.
6. [Connect your systems](/build-book/06-connect-your-systems): built in connectors and external connectors.
7. [Verify and audit](/build-book/07-verify-and-audit): records you can check without trusting the server.
8. [Deploy and operate](/build-book/08-deploy-and-operate): production, keys, migrations, monitoring.
9. [Errors and troubleshooting](/build-book/09-errors-and-troubleshooting): what each answer means and what to do.
10. [Security model and limits](/build-book/10-security-model-and-limits): what is guaranteed, and what is not.

Reference: [every endpoint](/build-book/reference-endpoints), [every SDK method](/build-book/reference-sdk),
[every error code](/build-book/reference-errors).

## Versions

This edition describes the code on `main` as of 2026-10-01. The published SDKs are 1.6.0 (`@parmana/sdk` on npm,
`parmana` on PyPI), published 2026-10-11. Methods marked **1.5.0** need that version or later:
`policyInEffect` and `policy_in_effect`, `verifyParmanaRelease` and `verify_parmana_release`.

## Full Integration Overview

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/guides/full-integration-overview

<Info>
  This page is a map, not a replacement for the guides it links to. For the
  files a new connector needs, see `docs/connectors/BUILDING_A_CONNECTOR.md` in
  the repository.
</Info>

**A naming trap worth avoiding first:** this codebase has two different things called
"connector." [`@parmana/connector-sdk`](/integrations/overview) is a generic library with
reference mocks (`SapConnector`, `OracleConnector`, etc.) that never talk to a real system. The
connectors the default server actually registers and runs in production, HubSpot, GitHub,
Paytm and Slack, follow a different, simpler pattern documented in the
[Connector Development Guide](/integrations/connector-development-guide). Any other HTTPS
endpoint can be connected with no code at all, as an **external connector**: see [Connect any
external system](/guides/connect-any-external-system). This page covers both real paths.

## The four pieces

| #   | Piece                                      | Answers                                                       | Exists independently of the others?                                                                                                           |
| --- | ------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | **A policy** bound to a capability         | Should this request be allowed?                               | Yes. It decides with no connector or caller wired to it. Every approve rule needs a signed human approval.                                    |
| 2   | **A caller (agent)** with a scoped API key | Who's allowed to even ask?                                    | Yes. It gets real decisions with no connector registered.                                                                                     |
| 3   | **A connector** for the capability         | Who performs the real world action once approved?             | Yes. A built in one is testable alone with `MockConnector`; an external one is your own endpoint.                                             |
| 4   | **A `SignalStateVerifier`**                | Are the caller's claims about real world state actually true? | The human approval is always verified this way. Other facts are checked only where a verifier exists (HubSpot deal state, the Slack channel). |

They're deliberately decoupled. That's why "got `APPROVED`" and "the action actually
happened" are two separate, independently verifiable claims (see
[Connect an Agent](/guides/connect-an-agent), Step 8).

## Recommended build order

1. **Write the policy first**, see [Write Your First Policy](/guides/write-your-first-policy).
   Everything else needs the exact capability string and `signalsSchema` up front.
2. **Onboard a caller and test authorization with no connector yet**, see
   [Connect an Agent](/guides/connect-an-agent). A `503 CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED` at this
   stage is expected: the policy approved, and nothing was executed.
3. **Connect the target system:** register your endpoint as an external connector ([Connect any
   external system](/guides/connect-any-external-system)), or build a built in connector
   ([Connector Development Guide](/integrations/connector-development-guide)).
4. **Add a `SignalStateVerifier` only if a caller lying about a signal is a real risk** for this
   capability that a policy rule alone can't catch. Built in connectors only.

## What breaks if you skip a piece

Every row here is a real failure mode this codebase has actually hit and diagnosed, several the
same night integrating a real refund agent partner.

| You have                                                  | Missing               | What happens                                                                                                                                          |
| --------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Policy + caller key                                       | Connector             | Approved, then `503 CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED` before release. Nothing was executed.                                                                   |
| Connector + caller key                                    | Policy                | `404` (`Policy '<name>' version '<version>' was not found.`). Never reaches your connector.                                                           |
| Policy + connector                                        | Caller key or scoping | `401`, or `403 CAPABILITY_NOT_ALLOWED`, or `403` (principal not permitted).                                                                           |
| All three                                                 | `SignalStateVerifier` | Works, but a caller's false claim about an unverified fact is trusted. A named, accepted scope limit; the signed human approval still has to be real. |
| Everything, but the deployment's signing config is broken | Nothing               | `503 SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE` before release. An operator problem none of the four pieces can fix from outside.                                           |

## Authorize and Execute an Action End to End

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/guides/authorize-and-execute

<Info>
  **[AVAILABLE]**, every command below runs against the repo's actual code.
</Info>

## Goal

See every stage of [how Parmana thinks](/how-parmana-thinks) fire for one real transaction:
policy decision, the signed authorization envelope itself (not just its effects), gateway
re-verification, and the resulting trust record.

## Prerequisites

- Completed [Quickstart](/quickstart) once, or at least read it, this guide assumes the
  server and keys are already set up the same way.
- Read [Execution authorization](/concepts/execution-authorization), this guide shows the
  envelope that page describes.

## Steps

### 1. See the authorization envelope directly

Over HTTP, the envelope comes back inside the Trust Record, in its `authorization` field,
after [the gateway](/concepts/the-gateway) has verified and consumed it. To see it produced
step by step, use the Runtime library directly, which is what
`examples/tutorials/11-execution-authorization/run.ts` does: build a `Runtime` with a
`FilePolicyRepository`, execute a transaction, and print `result.context.authorization`.

```bash
node_modules/.bin/tsx examples/tutorials/11-execution-authorization/run.ts
```

Real output (run again on 2026-10-02):

```
Authorization Summary
Payload Version  : 1
Authorization ID : 30c915ca-4516-459f-aae3-b501b40cd2f1
Decision ID      : 8e04698b-d56c-4974-a8be-57903907058f
Transaction ID   : txn-000001
Policy           : vendor-payment@2.1.0
Algorithm        : ed25519
Key ID           : default
Authorized At    : 2026-10-02T10:35:53.219Z
Expires At       : 2026-10-02T10:37:53.219Z
Nonce            : 888534f5-6bb0-43b4-b32c-270f26c58bf1
Content Hash     : 69b1858cd12ceeee715c5d90e22e68e1f1466a7047c3c7fdbb8056a434b5ec93
```

`Content Hash` is `businessTransactionHash`, the field [The gateway](/concepts/the-gateway)
independently recomputes and compares before releasing execution. `Expires At` is two
minutes after `Authorized At`, the envelope's TTL.

### 2. Run the same shape of request through the full server

This library call skips the gateway and connector entirely, it's the Runtime in isolation.
To see the _whole_ pipeline, authorization through gateway verification through credential
issuance through a connector, run [Quickstart](/quickstart) steps 3 and 5 if you haven't:
start the server, then execute a transaction over HTTP.

```bash
PARMANA_STORAGE=memory PARMANA_POLICY_DIR=/absolute/path/to/policies NODE_ENV=test npm run dev
```

```python
trust_record = client.execution.execute(transaction)
```

## Verify

Compare what each path returns. The library call above hands you the
`SignedExecutionAuthorization` on its own. The HTTP call hands you the final
`ExecutionTrustRecord`, which carries the same envelope in `authorization` (with its
`payload`: `authorizationId`, `nonce`, `policyContentHash`, `signalsHash`, `expiresAt`,
`businessTransactionHash` and the rest) and covers it with the record's signature. Both paths
produce a record whose `executions[0].decision.outcome` is `"APPROVED"` for the same input
signals and policy.

## Troubleshoot

- **`Execution Authorization was not generated` thrown by the tutorial.** The transaction's
  Decision came back `REJECTED`, an authorization is signed only after approval, see [Write
  your first policy](/guides/write-your-first-policy) for what a rejected decision actually
  does (it throws, it doesn't return a `REJECTED` object).
- **The HTTP path's trust record has no `authorization` field.** Records created before the
  field was added have none; every new approved record has it.
- **`Content Hash` differs between two runs with identical-looking transaction JSON.** Check
  timestamps and generated IDs (`businessTransactionId`, `intentId`, etc.), the hash covers
  the full executable content, any field that differs between runs changes it.

## Next

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Detect tampering" icon="bug" href="/guides/detect-tampering">
    Mutate this same content and watch the hash comparison reject it.
  </Card>
  <Card
    title="Verify a trust record independently"
    icon="check-double"
    href="/guides/verify-independently"
  >
    Check the resulting trust record's signature without Parmana running at all.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

## Human approval

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/concepts/human-approval

**No AI agent action is authorized without a signed human approval. Reads included.** A
refund, a merge, a Slack post, a HubSpot update, reading a pull request or a deal: each runs
only when a trusted person has signed an approval for that action, on that resource, and the
approval has not expired or been used.

People also approve policies before those policies can authorize anything, and review every
refused request. Parmana does not hold a request while it waits for a person: a refused request
stays refused, and the agent sends a new one with the approval attached.

| What a person does                                  | Status                                 |
| --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Sign an approval for every agent action, reads too  | **[REQUIRED]**                         |
| Approve a policy before it can authorize anything   | **[AVAILABLE]**                        |
| Review refused requests                             | **[AVAILABLE]**                        |
| Get notified when a request waits for an approval   | **[AVAILABLE]**, when a webhook is set |
| Add or revoke an approver without a deploy          | **[AVAILABLE]**                        |
| Approve a refused request so that same request runs | **[NOT AVAILABLE]**                    |

## Every action needs a signed approval

Two checks enforce this in code, for every policy and every action:

- **When a policy loads.** Every rule that approves must require one of the policy's
  `approvalSignals` with `is_true`, either as its whole condition or directly inside its top
  level `all`. A policy with any other approve rule fails to load, so every request under it is
  refused with `400` and `approves without a signed human approval`. A proposed policy change of
  that shape is refused the same way, so it cannot get through policy governance either.
- **When a request is decided.** A signal in `approvalSignals` counts as true only with a valid
  signed approval in the request: from a trusted, unrevoked approver, for this action and this
  resource (and amount, where the policy names one), not expired, used once. A runtime with no
  approval verifier configured refuses every approval instead of trusting the signal.

An agent that sets the approval signal to `true` without a signed approval is refused, whatever
else it declares. Tutorials 119 to 122 in `examples/tutorials/` show it step by step, for a
refund, the rule itself, a read, a Slack post and a HubSpot update.

| Action                | Policy in the binding       | The approval covers         |
| --------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------- |
| `paytm:refund`        | `customer-refund` 1.2.0     | the order, up to the amount |
| `github:pr-merge`     | `github-pr-approval` 1.1.0  | the pull request            |
| `github:pr-fetch`     | `github-pr-read` 1.1.0      | the pull request            |
| `hubspot:deal-update` | `hubspot-deal-update` 1.1.0 | the deal                    |
| `hubspot:deal-fetch`  | `hubspot-deal-read` 1.0.0   | the deal                    |
| `slack:post-message`  | `slack-post-message` 1.1.0  | the channel                 |

The reference policies with no connector need one too, for the Intent's `target`:
`vendor-payment` 2.1.0, `access-control` 1.1.0, `agent-vendor-payment` 1.1.0,
`api-key-issuance` 1.1.0, `connector-capability` 1.1.0, `database-change` 3.1.0,
`expense-reimbursement` 1.1.0, `production-deployment` 1.1.0, `rag-document-access` 1.1.0 and
`llm-tool-call` 1.1.0. The payment and expense policies also cover the amount. Older versions
that approved without a person stay in the repository as history and are refused when they load.

<Note>
  Production runs the version most recently approved through policy governance.
  Every version in the table and list above was approved in production on
  2026-09-30 and is in effect. Ask the server which version applies to an action
  with `GET /policies/in-effect?capability=<capability>`, and send that version.
</Note>

## Approve policies

In production, a policy authorizes nothing until one person proposes it and a second person
approves it with a signed step up authorization. The same person cannot do both. The whole
process, with commands, is in [Policy lifecycle and approvals](/guides/policy-lifecycle-and-approvals).

## Approve a refund

The `customer-refund` 1.2.0 policy authorizes a refund only with a signed approval from a
manager:

| Refund amount     | What it needs                    |
| ----------------- | -------------------------------- |
| 0 or less         | Refused                          |
| Above 0 to 100000 | A signed approval from a manager |
| Above 100000      | Refused, even with an approval   |

Why every refund: the agent declares `refundEligible` and `fraudCheckPassed` itself, and
nothing checks them. In 1.1.0 a refund up to 10000 was authorized on those two claims alone, so
an agent manipulated by prompt injection could approve its own refunds (G-75). In 1.2.0 they can
only refuse a refund.

<Note>
  `customer-refund` 1.2.0 has been in effect in production since 2026-09-28. A
  refund of any amount without a signed manager approval is refused with `403
  POLICY_DENIED`. There is no amount below which a refund runs on its own.
</Note>

The flow for a refund of 75000 on order `ORD-1042`:

<Steps>
  <Step title="The agent's request is refused">
    The agent sends the refund with `managerApproved: false`. Parmana refuses it with `403
    POLICY_DENIED`: the refund needs a signed manager approval. Nothing is
    executed, and a signed [Refusal Record](/concepts/refusal-records) is stored.
  </Step>
  <Step title="A manager reviews it">
    The manager finds the refusal, for example with the query in
    [Review refused requests](#review-refused-requests).
  </Step>
  <Step title="The manager signs an approval, on their own machine">
    <CodeGroup>

    ```bash Script
    npx tsx scripts/sign-approval.ts \
      --private-key-file ~/.parmana/manager-priya__manager-priya-key-1.private.pem \
      --approver-id manager-priya --key-id manager-priya-key-1 \
      --capability paytm:refund --resource-id ORD-1042 --max-amount 75000 \
      --out approval.json
    ```

    ```typescript TypeScript
    import { readFileSync, writeFileSync } from "node:fs";
    import { signApproval } from "@parmana/sdk";

    const approval = signApproval({
      privateKeyPem: readFileSync("manager-priya__manager-priya-key-1.private.pem", "utf8"),
      approverId: "manager-priya",
      keyId: "manager-priya-key-1",
      capability: "paytm:refund",
      resourceId: "ORD-1042",
      maxAmount: 75000,
    });
    writeFileSync("approval.json", JSON.stringify(approval));
    ```

    ```python Python
    import json
    from pathlib import Path
    from parmana.crypto import sign_approval

    approval = sign_approval(
        private_key_pem=Path("manager-priya__manager-priya-key-1.private.pem").read_text(),
        approver_id="manager-priya",
        key_id="manager-priya-key-1",
        capability="paytm:refund",
        resource_id="ORD-1042",
        max_amount=75000,
    )
    Path("approval.json").write_text(json.dumps(approval))
    ```

    </CodeGroup>

    The approval is for this order only, for refunds up to 75000, valid for 15 minutes
    (`--ttl-seconds` or `ttlSeconds` changes it, up to a day), and can be used once. The SDKs
    need no clone of the repository; the private key never leaves the process.

  </Step>
  <Step title="The agent sends a new request with the approval">
    A new `businessTransactionId`, the same order and amount, `managerApproved: true`, and the
    contents of `approval.json` in `signals.approvalArtifact`:

    ```json
    "signals": {
      "refundEligible": true,
      "fraudCheckPassed": true,
      "refundAmount": 75000,
      "managerApproved": true,
      "approvalArtifact": { "payload": { "...": "..." }, "signature": { "...": "..." } }
    }
    ```

  </Step>
  <Step title="Parmana verifies the approval and executes">
    Before authorizing, Parmana checks that the approval is signed by a trusted approver, has
    not expired or been revoked, is for `paytm:refund`, for this order (the Intent's
    `parameters.orderId`), covers this amount (the Intent's `parameters.amount`), and has not
    been used before. The gateway runs the same checks again just before release. Then the
    refund runs. The policy says which order and amount to check, in its `approvalSignals`
    (see [Add an approval to any action](#add-an-approval-to-any-action)).
  </Step>
</Steps>

`managerApproved: true` without a valid approval is refused, at any amount:

```text
Execution rejected: Rejected: declared signal(s) do not match independently verified state (managerApproved=true != verified managerApproved=false).
```

The same happens for an approval for another order, a smaller amount, another action, a
changed payload, an unknown or revoked approver, an expired approval, or one already used.

## Set up an approver

An approver is a person with an Ed25519 key pair. The private key stays on their machine; the
server trusts the public key. Add one through maker checker, with no deploy:

<Steps>
  <Step title="The approver creates a key pair on their own machine">

    ```bash
    npx tsx scripts/generate-approver-key.ts --approver-id manager-priya --key-id manager-priya-key-1 --out-dir ~/.parmana
    ```

    They send the public key file, `manager-priya__manager-priya-key-1.public.pem`, to a proposer.

  </Step>
  <Step title="One person proposes trusting it">
    `POST /approval-issuers/changes` with `action: "add"`, the ids, the public
    key and a reason.
  </Step>
  <Step title="A different person approves it">
    `POST /approval-issuers/changes/{id}/approve` with a step up authorization.
    The key is trusted from the next request on.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The full walkthrough, with rotation, revocation and errors, is
[Manage approvers](/guides/manage-approvers).

<Tip>
  To try the flow without a key pair, use the public sandbox: `POST
  /sandbox/approvals` signs a demo approval for `sandbox:receipt`, valid 300
  seconds. See [Playground](/playground). It exists only in the sandbox.
</Tip>

Approvers can also be listed in the server code, `TRUSTED_APPROVAL_ISSUERS` in
`packages/api/src/bootstrap/codeApprovalIssuers.ts`. Those change only with a pull request and a
deploy. The code list is checked first.

<Info>
  The hosted deployment's code list holds one key, `manager-charak1987-key-1`,
  revoked on 2026-09-30; its current approver key was added through maker
  checker. Approver keys are always Ed25519, whatever signing algorithm the
  server itself uses.
</Info>

## Add an approval to any action

A policy declares which of its signals need a signed approval in `approvalSignals`, with a path
to the resource in the Intent and, optionally, a path to a number the approval must cover. For
a merge that needs a release manager:

```json
"approvalSignals": {
  "releaseManagerApproved": { "resourceId": "target" }
}
```

A rule then reads the signal like any other, for example `{ "fact": "releaseManagerApproved",
"operator": "is_true" }`. The approver signs without `--max-amount`, since there is no amount;
the approval then names exactly this pull request, `acme/api#42`:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/sign-approval.ts   --private-key-file ~/.parmana/lead-sam__lead-sam-key-1.private.pem   --approver-id lead-sam --key-id lead-sam-key-1   --capability github:pr-merge --resource-id "acme/api#42" --out approval.json
```

The change goes live like any policy change: a new version, proposed and approved through
policy governance. It takes effect when it is approved, with no code change and no deploy. One
thing still needs a deploy: binding a built in connector's action to a different policy name. An
action registered as an [external connector](/guides/connect-any-external-system) names its
policy in its registration, through maker checker, with no deploy. Approvers are added
through [Manage approvers](/guides/manage-approvers).

Rules for a declaration, checked when the policy loads:

- `resourceId` is `"target"` (the Intent's target, such as `acme/api#42` for a pull request) or a
  path into the Intent's `parameters`, such as `parameters.orderId`. A number is compared as its
  decimal string. `value` is a path into `parameters` to a number.
- The approval's `scope.field` must be `value` when the declaration gives a `value`, and
  `resourceId` when it does not. The SDKs' `signApproval` and `scripts/sign-approval.ts` write
  these names. An approval scoped to any other field is refused, even when its bound would
  compare true.
- The key must be read by a rule, and must not also be in `boundSignals`.
- With more than one approval signal, give each its own `artifact`, the signal that carries its
  approval. The default is `approvalArtifact`.

## Approve a HubSpot update or read

`hubspot-deal-update` 1.1.0 authorizes every deal update only with `dealUpdateApproved: true`
and a signed approval for that deal in `signals.approvalArtifact`, whatever the amount. Sign it
with `--capability hubspot:deal-update` and the deal id as `--resource-id`, without
`--max-amount`. The dealstage transition is still checked against the real deal, and a
transition that is not allowed is refused even with an approval.

Reading a deal (`hubspot:deal-fetch`) has its own policy, `hubspot-deal-read` 1.0.0. It needs
`readApproved: true` with an approval for that deal, signed with `--capability
hubspot:deal-fetch`.

Under 1.0.0 an update within the amount threshold needed no person, and only a larger amount
change needed `preAuthorizedForAmountChange` with an approval. 1.0.0 now fails to load.

## Review refused requests

Every request that a policy refuses is stored with a signed
[Refusal Record](/concepts/refusal-records). To list recent refunds that were refused:

```sql
select
  refusal_record_id,
  business_transaction_id,
  submitted_by,
  created_at,
  decision_json ->> 'reason'                   as reason,
  evaluated_intent_json -> 'parameters'        as parameters
from refusal_records
where decision_json -> 'policy' ->> 'name' = 'customer-refund'
order by created_at desc
limit 50;
```

To list only the refunds waiting for a manager, add
`and decision_json ->> 'matchedRuleId' = 'reject-manager-approval-required'`.

Requests refused before policy runs, such as a failed authentication or a capability the caller
is not allowed to use, are in `caller_audit_events`:

```sql
select occurred_at, caller_id, capability, type, reason
from caller_audit_events
where type in (
  'caller.rejected',
  'caller.capability_denied',
  'caller.principal_denied',
  'caller.non_human_denied',
  'caller.structural_rejected'
)
order by occurred_at desc
limit 50;
```

<Warning>
  A Refusal Record is written after the request is refused, and a failed write
  does not change the refusal. A query can therefore miss a refused request.
  Each miss is logged as `refusal_record_write_failed`.
</Warning>

## Get notified

The full guide, with receiver code in Node.js and Python, is
[Approval notifications](/guides/approval-notifications).

Set `APPROVAL_WEBHOOK_URL` and `APPROVAL_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, and Parmana POSTs an event to that URL
each time a request is refused **only** for want of an approval: the policy declares
`approvalSignals`, and the same request with those signals true would have been authorized. A
refund refused for a failed fraud check, or above the maximum, sends nothing.

```json
{
  "type": "approval.needed",
  "occurredAt": "2026-09-29T10:15:02.114Z",
  "businessTransactionId": "5f0c...",
  "decisionId": "a91e...",
  "action": "paytm:refund",
  "target": "paytm://orders/ORD-1042",
  "policyId": "customer-refund",
  "policyVersion": "1.2.0",
  "reason": "...",
  "approvals": [
    { "signal": "managerApproved", "resourceId": "ORD-1042", "value": 75000 }
  ]
}
```

`approvals` is what to sign: `--capability` is `action`, `--resource-id` is `resourceId`, and
`--max-amount` is `value` when there is one. The event carries nothing else from the request.

Each request has two headers. `parmana-webhook-timestamp` is Unix seconds.
`parmana-webhook-signature` is `v1=` and the lowercase hex HMAC SHA256, keyed with the secret,
of the timestamp, a dot, and the exact body. Check it before acting, and refuse an old
timestamp:

```typescript
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from "node:crypto";

function isFromParmana(
  secret: string,
  timestamp: string,
  body: string,
  signature: string,
) {
  const expected =
    "v1=" +
    createHmac("sha256", secret).update(`${timestamp}.${body}`).digest("hex");
  const fresh = Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(timestamp)) < 300;
  return (
    fresh &&
    expected.length === signature.length &&
    timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(expected), Buffer.from(signature))
  );
}
```

Delivery is best effort: one attempt, at most 3 seconds, no retry. A failed delivery is logged
as `approval_needed_notification_failed` and changes nothing about the refusal. The refused
requests query above stays the complete list.

## Not available

**A refused request cannot be approved afterwards.** A policy decision is approve or refuse.
Nothing waits for a person. After a manager signs an approval, the agent sends a new request.

**Eligibility and fraud signals are still the caller's word.** `refundEligible` and
`fraudCheckPassed` are not checked against another system (G-51 in
`docs/VERIFICATION-GAPS.md`). They can only refuse; the signed approval authorizes.

**An approval covers the action and the resource, not every parameter.** An approval for a
Slack channel does not fix the message text, and an approval for a HubSpot deal does not fix the
new amount or stage. The approver trusts the agent with those details for that one use. An
approval for a payment, an expense or a refund does cover the amount.

**There is no automatic path.** No action is authorized without a person, by design. Adding one
would need a server side check that reads the facts itself, and a change to this rule
(G-80 in `docs/VERIFICATION-GAPS.md`).

## Why each action is bound to one policy

Each request names the policy that should judge it. If Parmana accepted any approved policy, a
caller could send a refund and name a policy written for Slack messages, which has no refund
limit. So each live action is bound to one policy name:

```text
paytm:refund         ->  customer-refund
github:pr-merge      ->  github-pr-approval
github:pr-fetch      ->  github-pr-read
hubspot:deal-update  ->  hubspot-deal-update
hubspot:deal-fetch   ->  hubspot-deal-read
slack:post-message   ->  slack-post-message
```

For a built in connector the name is fixed in code; for an external connector it is the
policy its active registration names (in the sandbox, `sandbox:receipt -> sandbox-receipt`).
The version is not fixed: in production it is the version most recently
approved through policy governance. Approving `customer-refund` 1.2.0 makes 1.2.0 the version
refunds must use, with no deploy, and approving 1.1.0 again rolls back. A request that names a
different policy, or any other version, is refused before any policy runs, with a message that
names the version in effect. Agents must then send that version.

---

## Connect an External Agent

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/guides/connect-an-agent

<Info>
  Covers the caller (agent) side. The repository's
  `docs/connectors/CONNECTING_AN_AGENT.md` points here. For what happens after
  approval (gateway, connector, the real business system), see [Connect any
  external system](/guides/connect-any-external-system), the [Connector
  Development Guide](/integrations/connector-development-guide) and
  `docs/connectors/PAYTM_CONNECTOR.md`.
</Info>

## The mental model

```text
AI Agent  --------------------------------------------------->  Parmana
   |  understands the request, extracts an intent                  |
   |  never decides whether the action is authorized                |
   v                                                                v
"I want to refund order X for ₹500"                    caller auth -> capability check
                                                         -> CapabilityPolicyBinder
                                                         -> SignalIntentBinder
                                                         -> PolicyEngine.evaluate
                                                         -> APPROVE or REJECT (binary, signed)
```

The agent proposes an intent. Parmana decides whether it's authorized. Only Parmana's decision can
unlock execution. If your integration ever lets the agent set a value that determines the outcome ,
an approval flag, a fraud-check result, a policy name, the model is broken, even if it "works."

## What you need, and why

| #   | You need                                                      | Why                                                                                                                                                         |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 1   | A reachable Parmana deployment                                | Nothing to connect to without one.                                                                                                                          |
| 2   | A capability name (e.g. `paytm:refund`)                       | Parmana authorizes capabilities, not free-form actions. Exact string matching, `refund` ≠ `paytm:refund`.                                                   |
| 3   | A deployed policy bound to that capability                    | Decides APPROVE/REJECT. Missing → `404`; a version other than the one in effect → `403 POLICY_DENIED`.                                                      |
| 4   | The policy's exact `signalsSchema`/`boundSignals`             | You must send every referenced signal; any `boundSignals` entry must equal the real `intent.parameters` value or the request is rejected before evaluation. |
| 5   | An API key scoped to exactly that capability                  | Your agent's identity, see below.                                                                                                                           |
| 6   | A trusted-signal source that is not the conversation          | Signals must come from an independent business system, never inferred from what the customer said.                                                          |
| 7   | Real UUID generation                                          | `businessTransactionId` is checked against a UUID shaped regex (versions 1 to 5); anything else is a `400` before any other logic runs.                     |
| 8   | A registered connector for your capability on this deployment | Without one an approved request is refused with `503 CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED` and nothing runs. See step 8 below.                                          |

## Step by step

**1. Read the policy file directly.** `cat policies/customer-refund/1.2.0/policy.json`; don't guess
field names from a description. Ask the server which version is in effect:
`GET /policies/in-effect?capability=paytm:refund`.

**2. Pick the exact capability string.** Case- and character-exact. This single detail is the most
common integration failure in practice.

**3. Mint a scoped API key:**

```bash
npx tsx scripts/generate-api-key.ts \
  --caller-id my-refund-agent \
  --allowed-capabilities "paytm:refund" \
  --credential-holder-type SERVICE
```

Use `SERVICE`, never `"AGENT"`, that value doesn't exist in `AuthorityType`. Never grant `"*"` to a
single-purpose agent; `/callers/me`'s `unrestrictedCapabilities` is literally
`allowedCapabilities.includes("*")`.

<Warning>
  **If you're the deployment operator adding this key** (not just the agent
  developer): `PARMANA_API_KEYS` is one environment variable holding a JSON
  **array**. Two real mistakes were made hand-editing a live deployment's value
  in a hosting dashboard: pasting the new entry as the *entire* value instead of
  appending it to the array (every caller gets a 500 until fixed, the server
  fails closed on malformed JSON), and losing existing entries by replacing
  rather than appending. Always paste the complete array, every existing entry
  plus the new one. Full account: the 2026-09-15 KMS migration troubleshooting
  guide (in git history).
</Warning>

**4. Verify the key before writing agent code:**

```bash
curl -i "https://<deployment>/callers/me" -H "Authorization: Bearer <key>"
```

If this fails, fix authentication first, nothing about your agent's request shape is relevant yet.

**5. Wire up real trusted-signal sources** for every field in the policy's `signalsSchema`. Not a
placeholder to fix later, from day one.

**6. Build the request:**

<Warning>
  **This example was missing `metadata` until 2026-09-14**, found while running
  [End-to-end: agent → Parmana → Paytm](/guides/end-to-end-paytm-flow) against a real
  deployment. Omitting it fails with
  `{"error":"metadata.businessTransactionId must match businessTransactionId."}` (400),
  before policy is ever evaluated. It's now included below.
</Warning>

```json
{
  "businessTransactionId": "<uuid v4>",
  "metadata": {
    "businessTransactionId": "<same uuid v4 as above>"
  },
  "authority": {
    "authorityId": "<uuid>",
    "authorityType": "SERVICE",
    "principalId": "my-refund-agent",
    "issuedAt": "<iso8601>"
  },
  "authorization": {
    "authorizationId": "<uuid>",
    "authorityId": "<uuid>",
    "purpose": "Authorize Paytm customer refund",
    "issuedAt": "<iso8601>"
  },
  "intent": {
    "intentId": "<uuid>",
    "authorizationId": "<uuid>",
    "action": "paytm:refund",
    "target": "<orderId>",
    "parameters": {
      "orderId": "<orderId>",
      "transactionId": "<txnId>",
      "amount": 500
    },
    "createdAt": "<iso8601>"
  },
  "policy": {
    "name": "customer-refund",
    "version": "1.2.0",
    "schemaVersion": "1.0.0"
  },
  "signals": {
    "refundEligible": true,
    "managerApproved": true,
    "fraudCheckPassed": true,
    "refundAmount": 500,
    "approvalArtifact": {
      "...": "the signed manager approval for this order and amount"
    }
  },
  "status": "RECEIVED"
}
```

`policy.name`/`policy.version` is never inferred from `intent.action`: name it explicitly, or a
caller could pair a real capability with an unrelated policy. Under `customer-refund` 1.2.0 every
refund needs a signed manager approval (G-75); without one the request is refused with `403
POLICY_DENIED`, whatever your agent declares about eligibility and fraud.

**7. Send it, handle the response**, see the complete reference table below.

**8. Confirm a connector is registered** for your capability on this deployment. A `200` means
the action was released and executed and its Trust Record signed; with no connector the answer is
`503 CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED` and nothing ran. To practise end to end with nothing installed, use
the public sandbox's `sandbox:receipt` ([Playground](/playground)). To connect your own system
without code, see [Connect any external system](/guides/connect-any-external-system).

**9. Verify independently**: `GET /refusal/:id` + `POST /refusal/verify` for a rejection,
`GET /trust-records/:id` (only once a connector is wired) for an execution, or fully offline with
`verifyExecutionTrustRecordOffline`.

## Complete response reference

Every row is what the server returns today (2026-10-02); the [Error
catalog](/api-reference/error-catalog) has every code.

| Status | `code`                                                | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                 | Do this                                                                                                                                        |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `200`  | none                                                  | Approved, released to the connector, executed, and the signed Execution Trust Record is the response.                                                                                   | Record the `trustRecordId`. This is the only answer that means the action ran.                                                                 |
| `400`  | none                                                  | Invalid `businessTransactionId`, malformed JSON, or a field that breaks the transaction's own rules.                                                                                    | Fix the request: the message names the field.                                                                                                  |
| `401`  | none                                                  | No key, or a key the server does not know.                                                                                                                                              | Check the key with `GET /callers/me`.                                                                                                          |
| `403`  | none                                                  | Your key may not assert this `authority.principalId`.                                                                                                                                   | Use your own `callerId`, or ask the operator for `allowedPrincipalIds`.                                                                        |
| `403`  | `CAPABILITY_NOT_ALLOWED`                              | `intent.action` is not in your key's `allowedCapabilities`. **The most common real bug.**                                                                                               | Compare `/callers/me`'s `allowedCapabilities` with your `intent.action`, character for character.                                              |
| `403`  | `POLICY_DENIED`                                       | The policy refused: a rule matched, the approval is missing, expired, for something else or already used, or the policy version is not the one in effect. The message names the reason. | Respect it. For a missing approval, get a signed approval and send a **new** request. Never retry with altered parameters.                     |
| `404`  | none                                                  | `policy.name` or `version` does not exist on this deployment.                                                                                                                           | Ask `GET /policies/in-effect?capability=...`.                                                                                                  |
| `409`  | none                                                  | `businessTransactionId` already used.                                                                                                                                                   | Read what happened to it, see [Idempotency](/api-reference/idempotency-and-nonces).                                                            |
| `429`  | `RATE_LIMITED`                                        | Too many requests for this key.                                                                                                                                                         | Wait for `Retry-After`, then retry the same request.                                                                                           |
| `502`  | `EXECUTION_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`                           | Released, but the call to the connector failed. It may have run.                                                                                                                        | **Do not send it again as a new transaction.** The operator checks the target system and resolves the intent.                                  |
| `503`  | `CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED`                            | Approved, but no connector serves this capability here. Nothing ran.                                                                                                                    | The operator configures the connector; then send a new request.                                                                                |
| `503`  | `SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE`, `EXECUTION_INTENT_UNAVAILABLE` | The server could not sign or store evidence before release. Nothing ran.                                                                                                                | Retry later with a new `businessTransactionId`.                                                                                                |
| `500`  | `EXECUTION_RECORD_INCOMPLETE`                         | Released, then the Trust Record could not be stored. The action ran.                                                                                                                    | **Do not send it again.** The operator finalizes the intent.                                                                                   |
| `500`  | none                                                  | Anything unexpected, including a gateway rejection of a tampered envelope.                                                                                                              | Ask the operator to read the server log before assuming your request was wrong.                                                                |
| (none) | none                                                  | Timeout or network error. Unknown whether Parmana received it; an approved request can take tens of seconds (G-84).                                                                     | Set the timeout to 120 seconds. After a timeout, read `GET /trust-records/{id}` and `GET /refusal/{id}` with the same id before anything else. |

## Common mistakes

- Capability string mismatch between `intent.action` and your key's `allowedCapabilities`.
- `authorityType: "AGENT"`, invalid; use `"SERVICE"`.
- A signal inferred from the customer's words instead of an independent business system.
- Treating `POLICY_DENIED` as a bug instead of a correct decision.
- Treating a timeout as a failure and sending the action again under a new id.
- Granting `"*"` "to get it working" and never narrowing it.
- Hand-editing `PARMANA_API_KEYS` by pasting a single entry instead of the complete array.
- Assuming a bare `500` means your request was wrong: ask for the server log first.

## Reference implementation

`pavancharak/parmana-phinite-agent` is a real, working implementation of every step above. Two bugs
were found and fixed in it: the exact `CAPABILITY_NOT_ALLOWED` mistake from the table above
(`"refund"` instead of `"paytm:refund"`), and error handling that crashed instead of resolving
unrecognized failures to an unresolved client-side state. See that repository's README for the full
writeup.

**Second round, entirely on Parmana's own side (2026-09-15/16):** after those agent-side fixes, this
same integration hit a sequence of purely Parmana-operator issues onboarding as a new caller on a
freshly KMS-migrated deployment: no `PARMANA_API_KEYS` entry at all (401) → a malformed hand-edited
entry (500 for every caller) → no `allowedPrincipalIds` grant for the asserted principal (403) → a
genuine Parmana-side bug where the gateway's signing and verification paths silently used different
keys after a KMS migration (500, unrelated to the request itself ,
`examples/tutorials/114-signing-verification-key-agreement/` reproduces it). None of these were agent
bugs. Full account: the 2026-09-15 KMS migration troubleshooting guide (in git history).
