## Run the server from source

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/deployment/local

<Info>
  **Running Parmana on your own infrastructure?** Use the [self hosted
  deployment](/self-hosted/overview): one Docker Compose command starts the
  server and its own Postgres, with keys, migrations and policies handled, and
  the [quickstart](/self-hosted/quickstart) takes you to a first signed
  decision. This page is for running the server directly from source, mainly for
  development.
</Info>

## What runs today

One Express process (`packages/api/src/server.ts`), single instance, no load balancer or
orchestration assumed. Signing keys are local PEM files read by `FileKeyProvider`. Storage
is either fully in-process (`memory`, non-persistent) or Postgres (`postgres`, or its older
name `supabase`; both use `DATABASE_URL`).

## Configuration

Real `.env` keys (from this repo, values redacted):

```bash
NODE_ENV=...
PORT=3000
PARMANA_STORAGE=postgres     # or: supabase (same thing), memory
HASH_PROVIDER=sha256
PRIMARY_SIGNATURE_PROVIDER=ed25519   # or: dilithium3 (needs Node >= 24)
KEY_PROVIDER=local
PARMANA_KEY_DIR=./keys
PARMANA_GATEWAY_KEY_ID=gateway       # optional, defaults to "gateway"
TRUST_PROFILE=v1
LOG_LEVEL=...                # read into config; gates @parmana/shared's createLogger/getLogger, not yet threaded through every console.* call site, see Roadmap
PARMANA_POLICY_DIR=...
HUBSPOT_PRIVATE_APP_TOKEN=...  # credential for the hubspot connector, omit to leave it unregistered
PARMANA_API_KEYS=...         # required, fails closed if unset, see Authentication
```

`PARMANA_KEY_DIR` is a single directory containing every keypair `FileKeyProvider` reads:
`default.*.pem` (authorization signing/verification) and `gateway.*.pem` (gateway
attestation, see [Gateway attestation](/concepts/gateway-attestation)). They are
deliberately separate keys in the same directory, not one key used for two purposes.
`PARMANA_GATEWAY_KEY_ID` lets you point the gateway at a differently-named key pair (for
example during rotation, run both `gateway` and `gateway-v2` side by side, then flip the
env var) without touching `default.*.pem` at all.

## Running it

```bash
NODE_ENV=test \
  PARMANA_STORAGE=memory \
  PARMANA_API_KEYS='[{"callerId":"demo","keyHash":"325ededd6c3b9988f623c7f964abb9b016b76b0f8b3474df0f7d7c23b941381f","allowedCapabilities":["test:fixture-execute"]}]' \
  npm run dev
```

`NODE_ENV=test` matters even though `PARMANA_STORAGE=memory` is set: two other components,
the Execution Gateway's replay-nonce store and the caller-authentication audit trail, default
to Supabase-backed implementations outside `NODE_ENV=test` (`createNonceStore.ts`,
`createCallerAuditSink.ts`) and will fail closed without a real, reachable Supabase project.
`PARMANA_API_KEYS` above is a demo key for local development only, raw key
`my-secret-api-key`, allowed to use `test:fixture-execute` and to act as `demo`. Its raw key is
public: make real keys with `npm run generate:api-key`, see [Authentication](/api-reference/authentication).

Generate the `default` and `gateway` keypairs first if you haven't, see
[Quickstart](/quickstart) step 2. Without it, the server refuses to start: the gateway is
wired unconditionally (see [The gateway](/concepts/the-gateway)), there is no code path that
skips needing this key.

## What this deployment does not give you

- **No self-service key management.** Caller authentication is real and fails closed (see
  [Authentication](/api-reference/authentication)), but issuing and rotating keys is an
  operator action (`scripts/generate-api-key.ts`), not an API call.
- **No KMS in this mode.** With `KEY_PROVIDER=local` your private keys, both
  `default.private.pem` and `gateway.private.pem`, are files on disk, exactly the exposure
  that produced the incident noted on [Security](/security/overview). Set
  `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms` to keep the `default` key in AWS KMS, see
  [AWS KMS signing](/deployment/aws-kms-signing).
- **Single process, single instance.** No HA, no load balancer assumed. Whether replicas
  share replay-nonce state depends on `NODE_ENV`: `MemoryNonceStore` (`NODE_ENV=test`, as
  above) is process-local, each process would accept the same authorization once, not once
  fleet-wide. Outside `NODE_ENV=test`, `SupabaseNonceStore` is durable and shared across
  replicas pointed at the same Supabase project, but this deployment shape is still one
  process behind no load balancer.
- **No connectors registered unless their credentials are configured.** HubSpot, GitHub,
  Paytm, and Slack each register only when their own environment variable is set
  (`HUBSPOT_PRIVATE_APP_TOKEN` and similar). See [The gateway](/concepts/the-gateway) for
  what adding a new connector requires.

## Node version

The Parmana server requires Node 24 or later. The root `package.json` sets `engines.node` to `>=24`, the
Dockerfile builds from `node:24`, and CI runs Node 24. Use Node 24 or later everywhere, including for
ML-DSA-65 (post quantum signing), which needs Node 24 or later for native `node:crypto` support. The TypeScript SDK
(`@parmana/sdk`) is separate and only needs Node 20 or later.

---

## Production deployment runbook

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/deployment/production

To run Parmana on your own infrastructure with one command, use the [self hosted deployment](/self-hosted/overview) instead. This runbook is for a hand built deployment, for example on Vercel with a Supabase database.

This runbook takes you from an empty environment to a server that is running, authenticated, governed and verified. Do the steps in order. Every step ends with a **Check**. Do not go to the next step until the check passes.

The exact meaning of every variable is in the [Environment variable reference](/deployment/environment-variables). If a startup error appears, look it up in the table at the bottom of that page.

## What you deploy

One container image, one process. `docker/entrypoint.sh` starts `node packages/api/dist/server.js` and forwards `SIGTERM` and `SIGINT` to it. There is no second process.

The same code also runs as a Vercel function, through `api/index.ts` and `vercel.json`. The steps below are the same on both. Section [Host specific steps](#host-specific-steps) lists the differences.

## Before you start

You need:

| You need                          | Why                                                                                                  |
| --------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A clone of the repository         | The scripts below run from the repository root.                                                      |
| Node and npm                      | The image uses Node 24. Run `npm install` once in the clone, then scripts run with `npx tsx`.        |
| A Postgres database               | Production storage. A Supabase project works. Note its **transaction pooler** connection string.     |
| A host for the container          | Fly.io, any Docker platform, or Vercel.                                                              |
| Two people, each with a human key | One proposes policy changes (the maker) and a different one approves them (the checker). See step 7. |

Production requires a real database, real signing keys and caller authentication. The server refuses to start without them, and it never falls back to something weaker.

## Step 1: Generate the signing keys

Run from the repository root:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/generate-keypair.ts --algorithm ed25519 --key-id default
npm run generate:gateway-keys
```

Both write into `./keys` unless `PARMANA_KEY_DIR` is set. They refuse to overwrite existing files unless you add `--force`.

**Check:** `keys/` contains `default.private.pem`, `default.public.pem`, `gateway.private.pem` and `gateway.public.pem`.

Never commit the private files and never bake them into the image. The image starts with an empty `keys/` directory on purpose. To keep the signing key inside AWS KMS instead, set `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms` and read the signing keys section of the environment reference. The gateway key is still a file.

## Step 2: Create the database schema

The server needs the tables in `supabase/migrations/`. Apply them with the tracked migration runner, from the repository root, with `DATABASE_URL` set to the production database. It applies each migration once, each in its own transaction, and records it in the table `parmana_schema_migrations`, so every later run applies only what is new.

```bash
npm run db:migrate -- status          # read only: lists applied and pending migrations
npm run db:migrate -- apply --dry-run # read only: lists what apply would run
npm run db:migrate -- apply           # applies the pending migrations
```

The first line of every command names the database it is using and whether it writes, for example `Database: db.example.supabase.co:5432/postgres as postgres (writes)`. `DATABASE_URL` is taken from your shell, or from the repository's `.env` file when the shell does not set it: check that line before you run `apply`.

**A database that already has the schema but no `parmana_schema_migrations` table** (it was set up with `scripts/apply-all-migrations.sql`, the Supabase SQL Editor or `supabase db push`) must be baselined once, so that `apply` does not run old migrations again:

```bash
npm run db:migrate -- baseline --through <the newest migration the database already has>
```

This records every migration up to and including that file as applied, without running any of them. Take the file name exactly as `status` lists it. Only baseline migrations the database really has.

<Warning>
  Do not run `scripts/apply-all-migrations.sql` on a database that holds data.
  It applies every migration again, several migrations drop and add back the
  same CHECK constraint, and a second run fails on rows written since
  (`docs/VERIFICATION-GAPS.md` G-61). It is only for a new, empty database,
  pasted into the Supabase SQL Editor.
</Warning>

**Check:** `npm run db:migrate -- status` ends with `0 pending`, and in the SQL Editor `select to_regclass('consumed_nonces'), to_regclass('execution_audit_events'), to_regclass('policies'), to_regclass('execution_intents'), to_regclass('approval_issuers'), to_regclass('external_connectors');` returns six names and no empty value.

<Warning>
  **Upgrading a deployment that already exists.** Apply new migrations
  **before** you deploy the version that needs them: `npm run db:migrate --
  apply`. Execution Intents are enforced by default and cannot be switched off
  in production, so a new version running without the `execution_intents` table
  refuses every execution with `503 EXECUTION_INTENT_UNAVAILABLE`. See
  [Execution
  Intents](/concepts/execution-intents#turn-it-on-the-deployment-order-matters).
</Warning>

If a request later fails with `PGRST205` ("Could not find the table"), the schema cache is stale. Run `NOTIFY pgrst, 'reload schema';` in the SQL Editor, or use Dashboard, Database, API, Reload schema cache.

## Step 3: Create the caller keys

Each caller gets its own key. Generate one for your first caller:

```bash
npm run generate:api-key -- --caller-id my-agent --allowed-capabilities paytm:refund
```

The command prints the raw key **once**, and a JSON entry. Give the raw key to the caller and store it nowhere else. Keep the JSON entry for step 5.

Make two human keys now, one for the maker and one for the checker, because step 7 needs both. **Every policy governance endpoint, including proposing a change, refuses a key that is not `credentialHolderType` `USER`.** A service caller such as `my-agent` cannot be the maker.

```bash
npm run generate:api-key -- --caller-id my-maker --credential-holder-type USER
npm run generate:api-key -- --caller-id my-checker --credential-holder-type USER --generate-step-up-key
```

The second command prints a bearer key, a step up private key, and a JSON entry. The checker keeps the bearer key and the private key. Only the JSON entries go to the server.

**Check:** you hold three JSON entries (the caller, the maker and the checker). Combine them into one array for `PARMANA_API_KEYS`, for example `[{...},{...},{...}]`. Each entry has a 64 character lowercase `keyHash`.

## Step 4: Decide the connector settings

A connector registers only when its settings are present. If you do not set a connector, the server still starts and every request for that connector's actions fails. For the refund connector set both of these, or neither:

| Variable                        | Value                                                    |
| ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `PAYTM_CONNECTOR_URL`           | The `https://` URL of your `parmana-paytm-agent` service |
| `PAYTM_CONNECTOR_SHARED_SECRET` | The shared secret that service expects                   |

The other connectors (HubSpot, Slack, GitHub) are in the [connector section of the environment reference](/deployment/environment-variables#connectors). To keep connector credentials in AWS Secrets Manager set `PARMANA_SECRETS_PROVIDER=aws-secrets-manager`.

## Step 5: Set the environment on your host

Set these in your platform, not in a file in the image. The minimum for production is:

| Variable             | Value                                                                                   |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `NODE_ENV`           | `production`                                                                            |
| `PARMANA_POLICY_DIR` | `./policies` (already set in the image)                                                 |
| `PARMANA_API_KEYS`   | The JSON array from step 3                                                              |
| `PARMANA_STORAGE`    | `supabase`                                                                              |
| `DATABASE_URL`       | Your Postgres connection string. Use the transaction pooler string on serverless hosts. |
| `PARMANA_KEY_DIR`    | `./keys`, with the four PEM files from step 1 mounted there                             |

If your host cannot mount files, set `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON` instead. It is a JSON object of the form `{"default":{"privateKeyPem":"...","publicKeyPem":"..."},"gateway":{...}}`. It writes any key file that does not already exist into `PARMANA_KEY_DIR` at startup.

Do not set `PARMANA_AUTH_DISABLED`. Do not set `NODE_ENV` to `test` or `development`. Do not set `SUPABASE_URL` or the other `SUPABASE_*` variables on the server, because it does not read them and only `DATABASE_URL` is used.

**Check:** the list of variables on your host includes all six from the table, and none of the two forbidden ones.

Optional: to notify approvers when a request waits for their approval, set `APPROVAL_EMAIL_TO` with the Resend integration, or `APPROVAL_WEBHOOK_URL` (https) and `APPROVAL_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, or both. See [Approval notifications](/guides/approval-notifications).

## Step 6: Deploy and confirm it started

Build and run the image:

```bash
docker build -t parmana-api .
```

Or use the image published with each GitHub release, `ghcr.io/pavancharak/parmana-api:<release tag>`. Check it with
`slsa-verifier` first and run it by digest, as shown in
[Verifying the server image](/security/overview#verifying-the-server-image).

Then start it on your host with the variables from step 5. The server validates every required setting before it opens the port. A wrong value makes it exit at once with a message that names the variable.

**Check** (replace `$URL` with your server's base URL):

```bash
curl -s "$URL/health"
curl -s "$URL/ready"
curl -s -o /dev/null -w "%{http_code}\n" -X POST "$URL/execute" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "{}"
```

The expected answers are:

| Request                     | Expect                                                                                                                                                   |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /health`               | `200` with `"status":"UP"`. This checks that the process is alive.                                                                                       |
| `GET /ready`                | `200` with `"status":"READY"` and `"authDisabled":false`. It runs `SELECT 1` against the database, and checks that the `execution_intents` table exists. |
| `POST /execute` with no key | `401` with a `WWW-Authenticate` header. This proves caller authentication is on.                                                                         |

Then read the startup log. The line `runtime_engine_constructed` must show `policyExecutionVerifierConfigured`, `signingReadinessConfigured` and `executionIntentsConfigured` all `true`: those are the policy approval check, the signing check before release, and the signed intent stored before release. They are on by default in production and cannot be switched off there.

If `/ready` returns `503` with `NOT_READY`, read the `reason`. Either the database is unreachable (check `DATABASE_URL` and the network path), or the `execution_intents` table does not exist (apply `supabase/migrations/20260921120000_add_execution_intents.sql` from step 2). If `authDisabled` is `true`, remove `PARMANA_AUTH_DISABLED` and redeploy at once.

## Step 7: Load and approve your policies

In production with Supabase storage, policies live in the `policies` table, not on disk. Do these two things.

**7a. Copy the policies into the database, once.** From the repository root, with `DATABASE_URL` and `PARMANA_POLICY_DIR` set in your shell:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/apply-policies-table-and-backfill.ts
```

It creates the `policies` table if needed and copies every policy found under `PARMANA_POLICY_DIR`. It prints one line per policy.

**7b. Give every policy a signed approval.** In production the gateway refuses to release an action for a policy that has no signed approval record whose hash matches the live policy. This gate is always on and cannot be switched off by a variable. Approve each policy you will use with the maker checker flow: the maker proposes it with their own key, and a different person, the checker, reviews it and approves it on their own machine with their step up key:

1. The maker: `POST $URL/policies/<name>/<version>/pending-changes` with the policy file, unchanged, as `proposedContent`.
2. The checker: `npx tsx scripts/local-review-action.ts --pending-policy-change-id <id> --action approve --private-key-file ./my-checker.step-up.private.pem --key-id my-checker --api-base "$URL"`, with their own key in `REVIEWER_KEY`.

Pass `--api-base` every time. Its default is a fixed address that is not your server. `--key-id` is the checker's caller id from step 3, and the private key file is the one that step printed. Do not use `scripts/refresh-approved-policy-content.ts` here: it proposes and approves in one process, so one person holds both keys and the approval record names a second person who did not decide.

The full procedure, and how to do it step by step by hand, is in [Policy governance: maker checker approval](/guides/policy-governance-maker-checker). Three rules matter here. The maker and the checker must be different callers. Both must have `credentialHolderType` set to `USER`. The checker also needs a step up public key.

<Warning>
  `scripts/backfill-legacy-policy-approvals.ts` can create approvals for every
  policy in one run under a fixed system identity. Those approvals are labeled
  as system approvals and do not record a human decision. Use it only if you
  accept that, and run it first without `--apply` to see what it would do. Never
  insert rows into `policy_change_approval_records` by hand: the table is the
  evidence of who approved what, and a hand written row cannot be told apart
  from a real approval afterwards.
</Warning>

**Check:**

```bash
export SUPABASE_URL="<your Supabase project URL>"
export SUPABASE_ANON_KEY="<your Supabase anon key>"
npx tsx scripts/verify-policy-changes-approved.ts --full-scan
```

This script is the one place that reads `SUPABASE_URL` and `SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, and it reads them from your shell, not from the server. That is deliberate: it uses the low privilege `anon` role, which can only read approval records, so a CI credential cannot write. It needs a Supabase project, because it uses the REST layer. On a plain Postgres, read `policy_change_approval_records` with SQL instead. It is fail closed. It exits with a non zero code if it cannot complete the check or finds a live policy with no matching approval record, and it reports each one.

## Step 8: Run one real request

Send one transaction that your policy approves, using the procedure in [Integrate Parmana: specification for AI agents](/agents/integrate) or one of the SDKs. Use a small, harmless action first.

The action needs a configured connector (step 4). Without one, the request still passes the policy and the approval check, and then stops at release with `503 CONNECTOR_NOT_REGISTERED` and nothing executed. Configure the connector, then retry with a new `businessTransactionId`.

**Check:** the response is the signed Execution Trust Record, and a repeat call with the same `businessTransactionId` returns `409`. Then verify the record independently with [Verify independently](/guides/verify-independently).

A `403 POLICY_DENIED` means the policy refused, which is a correct answer. A `503 SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE` or `503 EXECUTION_INTENT_UNAVAILABLE` means nothing was executed and you can retry later with a new `businessTransactionId`. A `500 EXECUTION_RECORD_INCOMPLETE` means the action was released, so do not resubmit it. A signed intent exists for it: read it with `GET /execution-intents/<businessTransactionId>`, and if its state is `RELEASED`, rebuild the record with `POST /execution-intents/<businessTransactionId>/finalize`. See [Execution Intents](/concepts/execution-intents) and [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting).

## Step 9: Turn on monitoring

Set up these before you send real traffic:

| Monitor                                                                                                                         | Alert when                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `GET /ready` every 30 seconds                                                                                                   | The status is not `200`, or `authDisabled` is `true`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Log event `rate_limit_store_not_durable`                                                                                        | It appears. It means rate limits are counted per instance, so `DATABASE_URL` is missing.                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| Response codes `503` with `SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE`                                                                                 | Any occurrence. The signing path is unhealthy and nothing is being released.                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Response codes `503` with `EXECUTION_INTENT_UNAVAILABLE`                                                                        | Any occurrence. The intent store or signing path is unhealthy and nothing is being released.                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| Response codes `500` with `EXECUTION_RECORD_INCOMPLETE`                                                                         | Any occurrence. An action was released with no signed record. Repair it with `POST /execution-intents/<id>/finalize`.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| Response codes `502` with `EXECUTION_OUTCOME_UNKNOWN`                                                                           | Any occurrence. An action was released and its connector call failed; its outcome must be checked and the intent closed with resolve. Several in a row mean the connector is down.                                                                                                      |
| `GET /execution-intents/unfinalized` (human credential), for example every 15 minutes                                           | Any entry in state `RELEASED`, which is a repairable released action with no signed record. Entries in `PREPARED` or `ERRORED` mean an action whose outcome must be checked at the connector, then closed with `POST /execution-intents/<id>/resolve`. A closed intent leaves the list. |
| Log events `execution_intent_prepare_failed`, `execution_intent_mark_released_failed`, `execution_intent_mark_finalized_failed` | Any occurrence. All are logged at critical severity.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| Log event `approval_issuer_lookup_failed`                                                                                       | Any occurrence. The `approval_issuers` table could not be read, so approvals from approvers added through [Manage approvers](/guides/manage-approvers) are refused until it can.                                                                                                        |
| Log event `approval_issuer_change_approved`                                                                                     | Every occurrence, as an audit trail: an approver key was added or revoked, with who proposed and who approved it.                                                                                                                                                                       |
| Log event `approval_needed_notification_failed`                                                                                 | Repeated occurrences. The approval webhook is failing; refused requests are still in the Refusal Records.                                                                                                                                                                               |
| Log level                                                                                                                       | Set `LOG_LEVEL=info`. Use `debug` only while investigating.                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

## Host specific steps

### Fly.io

`fly.toml` sets the app name, the primary region and a health check on `GET /ready` every 30 seconds.

1. Generate the secrets file without printing it: `node scripts/generate-fly-secrets.mjs`. It writes `.flysecrets/secrets.env` with `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON` and `PARMANA_API_KEYS`, and leaves the database values for you to fill in. Add `DATABASE_URL`, `NODE_ENV` and `PARMANA_STORAGE` to it.
2. Apply them: `fly secrets import < .flysecrets/secrets.env`.
3. Deploy: `fly deploy`.
4. Confirm with `fly status`. Every machine should show a recent update and a passing check. Machine placement is Fly's choice, so confirm the region there and do not assume the configured one.

Changing any secret restarts every machine. Treat the new value as live only after `fly status` shows passing checks.

### Vercel

The function entry is `api/index.ts`, configured by `vercel.json`. The policy files ship inside the function through `includeFiles`. The filesystem is read only, which is why production policies live in the `policies` table.

1. Set the variables from step 5 in the Vercel project for the Production environment. Use the Supabase transaction pooler string for `DATABASE_URL`.
2. Deploy to production, then run the checks in step 6 against your production URL.
3. Changing an environment variable needs a new deployment before it takes effect.

### Any Docker platform

Run the image with the variables from step 5, publish port `3000` (or set `PORT`), and mount the key files at `/app/keys` read only. Point the platform's health check at `GET /ready`.

## Agent network egress

Parmana checks the actions that go through it. An agent host that can open its own connections to a connector's API, or to any other system, bypasses every check. This happened in the October 2026 agent incidents: the models "used internet access in unintended ways" (Reuters, 2 October 2026).

Requirements for every host that runs an agent:

1. **Outbound traffic is allowed only to the Parmana endpoint.** Enforce this at the network layer: a firewall rule, a container network policy, or a sandbox with no default route. An application-level setting is not enough, because the agent can change it.
2. **No connector credential is present on an agent host.** Connector credentials (`HUBSPOT_PRIVATE_APP_TOKEN`, `PAYTM_CONNECTOR_SHARED_SECRET`, GitHub App keys and similar) belong only on the Parmana host. The agent holds its own Parmana caller key and nothing else.
3. **Check it.** From the agent host, each of these must fail, and the Parmana endpoint must succeed:

```bash
curl --max-time 5 https://api.hubapi.com/      # must fail: connection refused or timed out
curl --max-time 5 https://api.github.com/      # must fail
curl --max-time 5 https://<your-parmana-endpoint>/health   # must return 200
```

Denied connection attempts are not recorded as Parmana evidence today. Your network layer's logs are the only record of them. See `docs/REMAINING-WORK.md` section P for the open decision on reporting denied egress to Parmana.

## Shutdown and restarts

On `SIGTERM` or `SIGINT` the server stops accepting connections and lets in flight requests finish, then exits. `SHUTDOWN_TIMEOUT_MS` (default `10000`) is the longest a stuck request can delay that. Rolling restarts are safe, because the replay nonce store and the audit trails are always in the database and not in process memory.

## Rotating secrets

| To rotate            | Do this                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| -------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| A caller key         | Generate a new entry as in step 3, replace that caller's entry in `PARMANA_API_KEYS`, and redeploy. Give the caller the new raw key. The old key stops working when the new deployment is live.                                                           |
| The verification key | Run `npx tsx scripts/rotate-verification-key.ts --algorithm ed25519`. It creates a new key under a fresh id and prints the variable to set. Never delete the old key files, because records already signed with them are verified by their stored key id. |
| A connector secret   | Change the variable on your host, or the secret in Secrets Manager, then redeploy. Values are read once at startup.                                                                                                                                       |

## AWS KMS signing

Source: https://docs.parmanasystems.com/deployment/aws-kms-signing

With `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms`, Parmana signs inside AWS KMS. The private key is created in KMS and never leaves it. The server sends KMS the bytes to sign and receives a signature back.

This page takes you from no key to a verified deployment. Do the steps in order. Every step ends with a **Check**.

## What KMS signs, and what stays a file

| Signed with                                                                                | Where the key lives                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Execution Trust Records, Execution Intents, Refusal Records and audit event signatures     | The KMS key named by `PARMANA_VERIFICATION_KEY_ID`, alias `default` unless you set it         |
| Execution authorizations, receipts, policy change approval records and the execution chain | Always the KMS key with the alias `default`                                                   |
| The gateway attestation                                                                    | Still a file, `gateway.private.pem`, in `PARMANA_KEY_DIR` or from `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON` |

So a KMS deployment still needs the gateway key file. Only the `default` key moves to KMS. See the [Environment variable reference](/deployment/environment-variables#signing-keys-and-gateway-identity).

Only `KEY_PROVIDER` values `local` and `aws-kms` work. `azure-key-vault`, `gcp-kms` and `hsm` pass validation but have no implementation, and the server refuses to start with them.

## Before you start

| You need                       | Why                                                                                                                                                          |
| ------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| An AWS account and the AWS CLI | To create the key and the role. Sign in with a limited IAM user, not the account root user. See [Sign in with a limited user](#sign-in-with-a-limited-user). |
| A Vercel project               | The server reaches KMS from Vercel with short lived credentials (OIDC federation), so no AWS access key is stored anywhere.                                  |
| The repository cloned          | The verification script (`npm run verify:kms`) runs from it.                                                                                                 |

## Step 1: Create the key

The key must be an asymmetric Ed25519 signing key. The server accepts no other key spec and stops with `KmsSigner only supports ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 keys` if it finds one.

```bash
aws kms create-key \
  --key-spec ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 \
  --key-usage SIGN_VERIFY \
  --description "Parmana signing key" \
  --region ap-south-1
```

Note the `KeyId` in the output. Then give the key the alias the server looks for. The server turns the key id `default` into `alias/default`:

```bash
aws kms create-alias \
  --alias-name alias/default \
  --target-key-id <the KeyId from above> \
  --region ap-south-1
```

If you manage AWS with infrastructure as code, the CloudFormation resource `AWS::KMS::Key` takes the same `KeySpec` and `KeyUsage` values, and `AWS::KMS::Alias` creates the alias.

**Check:**

```bash
aws kms describe-key --key-id alias/default --region ap-south-1 \
  --query "KeyMetadata.[KeySpec,KeyUsage,KeyState]" --output text
```

You should see `ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 SIGN_VERIFY Enabled`.

The default region for this project is `ap-south-1`. Use one region everywhere, because `AWS_REGION` in step 3 must match the key.

## Step 2: Create the role that Vercel assumes

The server never holds an AWS access key. On Vercel it exchanges the project's OIDC token for short lived credentials by assuming an IAM role. Create a role with a trust policy and a permission policy.

**Trust policy.** It lets your Vercel project, and only it, assume the role. This is the format from the [Vercel OIDC documentation for AWS](https://vercel.com/docs/oidc/aws). Replace the four values in square brackets:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Principal": {
        "Federated": "arn:aws:iam::[AWS ACCOUNT ID]:oidc-provider/oidc.vercel.com/[TEAM SLUG]"
      },
      "Action": "sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity",
      "Condition": {
        "StringEquals": {
          "oidc.vercel.com/[TEAM SLUG]:sub": "owner:[TEAM SLUG]:project:[PROJECT NAME]:environment:production",
          "oidc.vercel.com/[TEAM SLUG]:aud": "https://vercel.com/[TEAM SLUG]"
        }
      }
    }
  ]
}
```

The OIDC identity provider `oidc.vercel.com/[TEAM SLUG]` must exist in your AWS account first. Create it as the Vercel documentation describes. Give the role the production environment only. Do not add `preview`, because a preview deployment should not sign with the production key.

**Permission policy.** Three actions on one key, and nothing else:

```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [
    {
      "Effect": "Allow",
      "Action": ["kms:Sign", "kms:GetPublicKey", "kms:DescribeKey"],
      "Resource": "arn:aws:kms:ap-south-1:[AWS ACCOUNT ID]:key/[KEY ID]"
    }
  ]
}
```

| Action             | Used for                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `kms:Sign`         | Signing, and the signing readiness probe that runs before an action is released             |
| `kms:GetPublicKey` | Publishing the public key at `/keys/default`, verifying signatures, and the readiness probe |
| `kms:DescribeKey`  | The startup check that the key exists, and reading its key spec                             |

Note the role ARN, which looks like `arn:aws:iam::[AWS ACCOUNT ID]:role/[ROLE NAME]`. You need it in step 3.

**Check:** in the IAM console, open the role and confirm the trust policy names your team and project, and the permission policy names your key.

## Step 3: Set the environment on Vercel

Set these for the **Production** environment. The full meaning of each is in the [Environment variable reference](/deployment/environment-variables).

| Variable       | Value                                               |
| -------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `KEY_PROVIDER` | `aws-kms`                                           |
| `AWS_REGION`   | `ap-south-1` (the region of the key)                |
| `AWS_ROLE_ARN` | The role ARN from step 2. It is a role, not a user. |

Keep the gateway key set as before, either files in `PARMANA_KEY_DIR` or `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON`. Do not set an AWS access key. The server never reads one.

Turn on OIDC federation for the Vercel project, as the [Vercel documentation](https://vercel.com/docs/oidc/aws) describes, so the function receives an OIDC token. Then deploy again, because variables are read once at startup.

**Check:** `vercel env ls production` lists all three variables.

## Step 4: Deploy and check the key is reachable

```bash
vercel deploy --prod
```

Then, with your base URL in `URL`:

```bash
curl -s "$URL/keys/default"
curl -s "$URL/ready"
```

The first call returns the public half of the KMS key:

```json
{
  "keyId": "default",
  "algorithm": "ed25519",
  "use": "sig",
  "pem": "-----BEGIN PUBLIC KEY-----\n...\n-----END PUBLIC KEY-----\n"
}
```

`/ready` should answer `{"status":"READY","authDisabled":false}`.

On Vercel the app is built on the first real request, not when the module loads, because the OIDC token only exists while a request is being handled. The first request after a cold start therefore does the setup work, including the call to KMS.

**Check:** `/keys/default` returns `"algorithm": "ed25519"`. A `500` here means the server could not reach the key. See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting).

## Step 5: Verify signing

The repository has a script that signs test data through the same `KmsSigner` the server uses, on both sides of the 4096 byte limit. It changes nothing in AWS. It makes about seven `kms:Sign` calls, one `kms:GetPublicKey` and one `kms:DescribeKey` per run.

Sign in with a limited user first (see [Sign in with a limited user](#sign-in-with-a-limited-user)), then run from the repository root:

```bash
AWS_REGION=ap-south-1 AWS_PROFILE=<your profile> npm run verify:kms
```

On PowerShell:

```powershell
$env:AWS_REGION = "ap-south-1"; $env:AWS_PROFILE = "<your profile>"; npm run verify:kms
```

Expected output:

```text
PASS  Key is an Ed25519 signing key  (algorithm ed25519)
PASS  Signs 300 bytes as they are  (commitment false, 300 bytes signed, verifies true)
PASS  Signs 4096 bytes as they are (the limit)  (commitment false, 4096 bytes signed, verifies true)
PASS  Signs 5000 bytes as a 97 byte commitment  (commitment true, 97 bytes signed, verifies true)
PASS  Signs 60000 bytes as a 97 byte commitment  (commitment true, 97 bytes signed, verifies true)
PASS  A signature does not verify over different data  (verifies false)
PASS  KMS refuses 5000 raw bytes (control)  (ValidationException: ... length less than or equal to 4096)

All 7 checks passed.
```

The last check is a control. It sends 5000 raw bytes straight to KMS and requires KMS to refuse them. It proves the limit is real and that the commitment is what makes larger messages work.

The exit code is `0` when every check passes. If `AWS_ROLE_ARN` is set in your shell, the script ignores it and says so, because that variable selects the Vercel OIDC token, which only exists on Vercel.

**Check:** the last line reads `All 7 checks passed.`

## Step 6: Verify a real record offline

Signing that verifies in a script is not the same as a record that a third party can check. Run one real request as in [Integrate Parmana: specification for AI agents](/agents/integrate). Save the Execution Trust Record it returns, and get the key from the server:

```bash
curl -s "$URL/keys/default" > key.json
```

Write the `pem` value into `default.public.pem`, then verify with only that public key:

```bash
npx tsx scripts/verify-trust-record.ts record.json default=default.public.pem
```

**Check:** the output has `"valid": true` and `"errors": []`. Verifying the same record against a different public key must fail. A full record is usually larger than 4096 bytes, so this also proves the commitment path end to end. The rule a verifier you write yourself must follow is in [Verify independently](/guides/verify-independently).

## How messages over 4096 bytes are signed

KMS refuses a raw Ed25519 message longer than 4096 bytes. A full Execution Trust Record is larger than that. Parmana signs a message over the limit as a fixed 97 byte commitment instead: the bytes `PARMANA-ED25519-LARGE-MESSAGE-V1`, one NUL byte, then the SHA-512 digest of the message. The result is still an ordinary Ed25519 signature. Messages of 4096 bytes or fewer are signed unchanged. No marker is stored on the record, because the choice depends only on the message length. The decision is recorded in ADR-0010 in `docs/adr`.

## Sign in with a limited user

Do not run checks as the AWS account root user. Use an IAM user that can do only what this page needs. A user with the three actions from step 2, on the one key, is enough to run `npm run verify:kms`. It does not need `iam:*`, and it should have no access keys.

Sign in with the console based login, which stores short lived credentials on your machine and needs no access key:

```bash
aws login --profile <your profile>
```

At the browser page choose **IAM user**, and enter the account ID, the user name and the password. Add the AWS managed policy `SignInLocalDevelopmentAccess` to the user, because `aws login` needs it.

**Check:**

```bash
aws sts get-caller-identity --profile <your profile>
```

The `Arn` should end in `user/<your user name>` and must not end in `:root`. Then confirm the user is limited: `aws iam list-users --profile <your profile>` should fail with `AccessDenied`.

<Warning>
  A second `aws login` with the same `--profile` replaces the credentials stored
  for that profile. If you use one profile for both root and a limited user, the
  last login wins. Give each its own profile name.
</Warning>

## Run the whole server against KMS locally

To reproduce a full request with KMS signing on your machine, start the server with these settings, on top of the minimum from the [production runbook](/deployment/production):

| Variable       | Value                                                                                 |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `KEY_PROVIDER` | `aws-kms`                                                                             |
| `AWS_REGION`   | `ap-south-1`                                                                          |
| `AWS_PROFILE`  | The limited profile from the previous section                                         |
| `AWS_ROLE_ARN` | **Not set.** A set value selects the Vercel OIDC token, which does not exist locally. |

The gateway key is still read from `PARMANA_KEY_DIR`. A connector that verifies the gateway's authorization, such as the refund service, must use the same key provider and the same KMS access, or it will report an invalid signature.

## Troubleshooting

| You see                                                                            | Cause                                                                                                                                                                                                              | Fix                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms is configured, but no KMS key named "default" is reachable`  | Wrong region, missing alias, or the role cannot describe the key                                                                                                                                                   | Check `AWS_REGION`, that `alias/default` exists in that region, and that the role has `kms:DescribeKey` on the key.                                                                                                                     |
| `KmsSigner only supports ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519 keys`                               | The key has a different key spec                                                                                                                                                                                   | Create the key as in step 1. A key's spec cannot be changed.                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `503` with code `SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE` and `AccessDeniedException` in the message   | The role lacks `kms:Sign` or `kms:GetPublicKey`, or the key is disabled                                                                                                                                            | Fix the permission or enable the key, then retry with a new `businessTransactionId`. Nothing was executed. See [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting).                                                                                     |
| `VercelOidcTokenError: The 'x-vercel-oidc-token' header is missing`                | Something called AWS while the module loaded, before any request                                                                                                                                                   | Use the current `api/index.ts`, which builds the app on the first request.                                                                                                                                                              |
| `ValidationException ... length less than or equal to 4096`                        | A build without the large message rule signed a message over the limit                                                                                                                                             | Deploy a build that includes ADR-0010, then run `npm run verify:kms`.                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `503` with code `EXECUTION_INTENT_UNAVAILABLE`                                     | The signed [Execution Intent](/concepts/execution-intents) could not be signed and stored before release. Under KMS the usual causes are the same as `SIGNING_UNAVAILABLE`, or a missing `execution_intents` table | Fix the permission or apply `supabase/migrations/20260921120000_add_execution_intents.sql`, then retry with a new `businessTransactionId`. Nothing was executed.                                                                        |
| `500` with code `EXECUTION_RECORD_INCOMPLETE`                                      | The action was released and the signed record could not be produced afterwards                                                                                                                                     | Do not retry as a new transaction. A signed Execution Intent exists, and an operator can rebuild the record without repeating the action. See [Execution Intents](/concepts/execution-intents) and [Troubleshooting](/troubleshooting). |
| `npm run verify:kms` says the session expired                                      | The local AWS login has expired                                                                                                                                                                                    | Run `aws login --profile <your profile>` again.                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| A record fails offline verification against your local key                         | It was signed by KMS, and your local `default.public.pem` is a different key                                                                                                                                       | Verify against the public key from `GET /keys/default`.                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| `AccessDenied` for `iam:` actions when you use the limited user                    | This is correct. The limited user has no such permission                                                                                                                                                           | Nothing to fix.                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `Gateway private key not found` or `Gateway public key not found`                  | The gateway attestation key is still a file, and KMS does not supply it                                                                                                                                            | Provide `gateway.private.pem` and `gateway.public.pem` in `PARMANA_KEY_DIR` or through `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON`.                                                                                                                     |
| The gateway rejects a real execution with `failed checks [signatureVerified, ...]` | Signing and verification are using different keys                                                                                                                                                                  | Check that the build includes the 2026-09-16 fix in `packages/api/src/bootstrap/createExecutionGateway.ts`, where the gateway verifies with the same KMS backed key provider the runtime signs with.                                    |
| A connector service reports only a generic HTTP 500                                | The real reason is recorded on the other side                                                                                                                                                                      | Query `execution_audit_events` by `business_transaction_id`. Both Parmana and `parmana-paytm-agent` write a `reason` there, see the [Database Schema Reference](/storage/schema-reference).                                             |

## Keep in mind

- Do not store a static AWS access key on Vercel for runtime signing. The OIDC role in step 2 exists so that no such key is needed.
- The code resolves the logical key id `default` to `alias/default`. A descriptive alias on the same key does not replace it.
- Keep `PARMANA_KEY_MATERIAL_JSON` (or the key files) after moving to KMS: it still carries the gateway key.
- A per tenant key `tenant.<id>` resolves to `alias/tenant/<id>`: KMS alias names cannot contain a dot, so each dot in a key id becomes a slash. To give a tenant its own key, create a separate KMS key with that alias, for example `alias/tenant/acme` for `tenant.acme`. Without the alias, that tenant's authorizations are signed with `default`. This mapping is covered by unit tests only; it has not been run against real AWS.
- Public keys and `DescribeKey` answers are cached in memory for 5 minutes per process. A failed or missing lookup is not cached. After repointing an alias to a new key, allow 5 minutes before records signed by the new key verify on every instance.
- A keyId is always a logical name such as `default`, or an `alias/` name. A full key ARN is refused, including one named by a record being verified.
- Keep `CRYPTO_MODE=single` (the default). Hybrid signing (Ed25519 and ML-DSA-65) uses local key files for both signatures, so the server refuses to start with `CRYPTO_MODE=hybrid` and `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms`.
- After the key exists, narrow the administrator's own policy. `kms:CreateKey` with no resource limit is more than day to day work needs.

## What has been verified

Verified on 2026-09-20, against a real KMS key (`alias/default`, `ap-south-1`, `ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519`, enabled), using a limited IAM user with only the three actions above:

| Check                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Result               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `npm run verify:kms`: messages of 300, 4096, 5000 and 60000 bytes signed and verified, a signature over other data rejected, and 5000 raw bytes refused by KMS                                                 | 7 of 7 pass          |
| The full server with `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms` signed an Execution Trust Record of about 5.6 KB (over the limit that failed in production on 2026-09-20), and it verified offline against the KMS public key only | Pass                 |
| The same record verified against a different key                                                                                                                                                               | Failed, as it should |
| Signing errors in the server log during the full run                                                                                                                                                           | None                 |

Verified again on 2026-09-21 for [Execution Intents](/concepts/execution-intents), with the same key and the same limited IAM user, through the production Docker image, a real Postgres and the real `parmana-paytm-agent` using fake Paytm staging credentials:

| Check                                                                                                                                                       | Result                                                                                                              |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| The full server with `KEY_PROVIDER=aws-kms` signed an Execution Intent before release, and signed the Execution Trust Record and the policy approval record | Pass                                                                                                                |
| The intent, and the Trust Record, each verified offline against the KMS public key only                                                                     | Pass, 23 of 23 checks in the first run and 37 of 37 in the final run, which added closing an intent by hand         |
| The extra `kms:Sign` for the intent                                                                                                                         | About 35 ms median (34 to 40 ms, 10 samples), from a Windows machine to `ap-south-1`. **Not measured from Vercel.** |

Each released action now costs **two** `kms:Sign` calls in the request, one for the intent and one for the Trust Record, plus the readiness probe at most once a minute per instance.

Not covered by those runs:

1. **The Vercel OIDC role.** The runs used the local AWS credential chain. ADR-0010 records the live production verification of the OIDC role for the Trust Record, and no run has exercised the OIDC role for the intent signature, although it uses the same signer and the same permissions.
2. **A real Paytm refund.** The agent chain ran with fake Paytm staging credentials, on purpose, so Paytm rejected the call. No refund was sent.
3. **Key rotation and other regions.** Neither was tested.
